title: Preparedness is a global public good with a domestic budget problem
source_unit: OECD, Tracking spending on prevention, preparedness and response to global health threats, 24 September 2026
geography: Global; high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income country groups; OECD Development Assistance Committee financing

observations.period: 2023; estimated health-sector prevention, preparedness and response spending by country-income group

health_budget_share.value: less than 2% of health expenditure in high-income countries versus about 10% in low-income countries

post_pandemic_path.value: PPR spending declined from the pandemic peak but remained, on average, 13% above 2019 levels as a share of GDP in 2023

mechanism.value: Preparedness capacity is distributed through sharply unequal fiscal spaces: poorer countries devote a larger share of constrained health budgets while spending far less per person

observations.method: OECD estimate mapping System of Health Accounts functions to Prevention, Preparedness and Response technical areas using Joint External Evaluation categories and country-income-group comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The estimates cover recurrent health-sector spending and do not capture all capital expenditure, medical-countermeasure R&D or relevant spending outside health, including animal health and agriculture; income-group averages conceal country variation.
observations.subgroup: People in low-income countries, health workers, public-health agencies, households exposed to outbreaks, and populations dependent on thin health budgets for routine and emergency protection.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher PPR shares in low-income countries may reflect urgent exposure and lower denominators rather than stronger preparedness; lower shares in high-income countries may coexist with substantial capabilities outside the measured health budget.

observations.period: 2023–2026; external financing and aid exposure for low-income-country PPR

denominator.unit: low-income-country PPR expenditure with available data

external_financing.value: external sources, including aid, financed nearly 75% of total PPR expenditure in low-income countries with available data in 2023

health_oda_projection.value: ODA for health from Development Assistance Committee countries is projected to decline by 29–46% between 2024 and 2026, equivalent to USD 5–8 billion

pandemic_peak_comparison.value: Projected health ODA in 2026 would be approximately 63% below its 2022 pandemic peak

mechanism.value: A globally shared protection system becomes fragile when frontline countries rely on external flows whose political priorities and fiscal cycles are set elsewhere

observations.method: OECD comparison of PPR financing sources and projected development-assistance trends, situated within the global-public-good logic of surveillance, infection prevention, emergency response and research.
observations.uncertainty: The projection is not a forecast of every donor or country flow and does not estimate the effect of each financing cut on outbreak probability, mortality, service continuity or national preparedness; external financing varies across countries.
observations.subgroup: Low-income-country health ministries and public-health workers, aid-dependent communities, regional surveillance networks, donors and populations in neighbouring countries that benefit from cross-border risk reduction.
observations.counterinterpretation: External financing can be catalytic and may support capabilities that domestic budgets would not create quickly; reduced aid does not necessarily imply reduced effectiveness if domestic or pooled financing replaces it.

observations.period: 2026 measurement and governance problem; tracking PPR across health and non-health sectors

measurement_gap.value: PPR spending is not systematically tracked in an internationally comparable way because relevant activities are embedded across multiple health and non-health sectors

scope.value: PPR includes surveillance, infection prevention and control, emergency response, R&D, antimicrobial resistance, chemical, nuclear and radiological events, and biotechnology- and AI-enabled biological risks

tracker.value: OECD, WHO, World Bank and partners are developing a Global Health and Resilience Tracker using System of Health Accounts and Creditor Reporting System standards

mechanism.value: What is hard to see in a budget is hard to defend politically: delayed and diffuse prevention benefits lose priority to immediate domestic demands unless measurement creates a shared account of resilience

observations.method: OECD methodological brief combining health-accounting attribution, international development-finance reporting standards and a policy analysis of global-public-good underinvestment.
observations.uncertainty: The tracker and attribution approach are designed to improve comparability but remain estimates; current measures omit several relevant sectors and cannot by themselves establish whether spending is adequate, well allocated or equitably governed.
observations.subgroup: Budget officials, public-health agencies, laboratories, animal-health and agricultural systems, technology and research institutions, civil society, donors and communities seeking accountable preparedness.
observations.counterinterpretation: More measurement can create administrative burden, encourage metric gaming or narrow preparedness to what fits existing accounting systems; visibility does not guarantee durable political commitment or effective delivery.

boundary: This record identifies a global-health-financing, preparedness and measurement subtheme. It does not establish that any particular spending level, aid reduction, tracker or domestic-financing reform will cause an outbreak, prevent one, improve health outcomes, strengthen sovereignty, or distribute protection equitably; those require named country, institution, workforce, household and outbreak episodes with observed budgets, capabilities, delivery, access and political response.
